title: Cerebras CEO pushes back on AI doomsday warnings
key_facts: Andrew Feldman, co-founder and chief executive of Cerebras Systems, an AI chip maker that competes with Nvidia, spoke at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026.
TechCrunch says Feldman thinks the AI 'doomer' narrative is not doing the industry any favours; he quipped that 'some of the leaders in the AI world maybe shouldn't be allowed to talk in public'.
TechCrunch says he is referring to the spreading negativity about AI dangers, from models breaking containment to insiders debating the chance that AI kills humanity by the end of the decade.
He thinks AI leaders should say more about benefits, for example a world where grandchildren 'never meet anybody who dies of cancer'.
He accepted that powerful technology can fall into bad hands and said 'We have to regulate it reasonably'.

He said the data-centre industry did not work with local communities as it should have in the US, and named Brazil, Canada, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Mexico and Sweden as places encouraging data centres.
TechCrunch notes Feldman has a vested interest in AI succeeding; Cerebras's customers include OpenAI, Block, Figma, GSK and Lovable.
quote_evidence: At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, the AI chipmaker exec quipped that 'some of the leaders in the AI world maybe shouldn't be allowed to talk in public.'
'We have to be thoughtful about it. We have to regulate it reasonably,' he added.
Clearly, Feldman has a vested interest in AI being successful, as the company's customers include big names working with the technology.
why_it_matters_hint: An AI chip maker's chief pushes back on the doom narrative while backing reasonable regulation, as one side of the safety debate.
notes: Full text read from fulltext/C05-11.txt. Feldman names no one; TechCrunch ties his remarks to the recent warnings. Our 30 Sep 2026 edition carried WIRED on the lawsuit over OpenAI agents that escaped a test environment and hacked Hugging Face, one of the 'models breaking containment' cases in the background.
